question: What is the primary trigger for a cardiac action potential across cell membranes?

options.A: Movement of ions like sodium and potassium
options.B: Release of stored oxygen molecules in the tissue
options.C: Sudden changes in the temperature of the blood
options.D: Direct stimulation by circulating red blood cells

explanation: Cardiac cells generate electrical activity by rapidly shifting ions like sodium, potassium, and calcium across their membranes. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T3#GNS223_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why does a reentry circuit cause an arrhythmia?

options.A: It forces the heart muscle cells to permanently stop receiving oxygen
options.B: It traps an electrical signal in a looping pathway that causes rapid contractions
options.C: It immediately destroys the natural pacemaker cells in the right atrium
options.D: It completely blocks all electrical impulses from leaving the sinoatrial node

explanation: A reentry circuit occurs when an electrical wave gets stuck traveling in a circle, constantly re-stimulating the heart tissue to beat too fast. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T3#GNS223_U1_T3_h1)

question: What is the main purpose of the Vaughan Williams classification system for nurses?

options.A: To group antiarrhythmic drugs by their primary electrophysiological effect on the heart
options.B: To determine the financial cost and manufacturing source of cardiac drugs
options.C: To calculate the exact safe dosage of medication based on patient body weight
options.D: To predict which patients will develop permanent heart failure within a year

explanation: The classification organizes drugs by how they alter the electrical currents and action potentials in cardiac tissue. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T3#GNS223_U1_T3_h2)

question: Which medication belongs to the Class IB sodium channel blocker group?
explanation: Lidocaine is a classic Class IB sodium channel blocker frequently used for treating acute ventricular arrhythmias. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T3#GNS223_U1_T3_h3)

question: Why must clinicians be very cautious when giving Class IC drugs to a patient with a history of a heart attack?

options.A: These drugs will immediately cause the patient's blood pressure to drop to zero
options.B: The damaged heart muscle will completely neutralize the drug within five minutes
options.C: Strong sodium blockade can provoke dangerous new arrhythmias in damaged heart tissue
options.D: Class IC medications only work when mixed with high doses of intravenous potassium

explanation: Class IC drugs slow conduction so drastically that they can cause fatal rhythm problems in structurally damaged hearts. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T3#GNS223_U1_T3_h3)

question: What is the primary receptor targeted by Class II antiarrhythmic drugs?
explanation: Class II drugs are beta-blockers that attach to beta-adrenergic receptors to block the effects of adrenaline on the heart. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T3#GNS223_U1_T3_h4)

question: Why should non-selective beta-blockers be used very carefully in patients with asthma?

options.A: They permanently destroy the tiny air sacs located at the base of the lungs
options.B: They cause the lungs to fill up with fluid within a few minutes of dosing
options.C: They stop asthma inhalers from working by coating the inside of the throat
options.D: They can block receptors in the lungs and trigger dangerous airway constriction

explanation: Non-selective beta-blockers affect receptors outside the heart, which can cause the smooth muscles in the airways to tighten. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T3#GNS223_U1_T3_h4)

question: How do Class III antiarrhythmic drugs primarily affect the cardiac action potential?

options.A: They stop all electrical signals from leaving the ventricles
options.B: They speed up the initial sodium influx to hasten contraction
options.C: They delay repolarization to lengthen the refractory period
options.D: They open calcium gates wide to increase pumping strength

explanation: By blocking potassium channels, these drugs keep the cell in a resting, refractory state longer, preventing chaotic signals. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T3#GNS223_U1_T3_h5)

question: What makes amiodarone different from most other antiarrhythmic medications?

options.A: It is completely cleared from the human body within two hours of a dose
options.B: It cannot be given intravenously under any emergency circumstances
options.C: It displays properties from all four Vaughan Williams classes of medications
options.D: It only works when taken alongside a high-fat meal to help absorption

explanation: Amiodarone is a broad-spectrum drug that blocks sodium, potassium, and calcium channels while also acting as a beta-blocker. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T3#GNS223_U1_T3_h5)

question: Which two medications belong to the Class IV calcium channel blocker group?
explanation: Verapamil and diltiazem are non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers used to control heart rates in SVTs. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T3#GNS223_U1_T3_h6)

question: Why are Class IV drugs effective for treating supraventricular tachycardia?

options.A: They completely eliminate all electrical activity in the heart wall
options.B: They speed up the natural pacemaker cells in the right atrium
options.C: They slow down conduction through the atrioventricular node
options.D: They force the ventricles to beat faster than the upper chambers

explanation: By slowing AV node conduction, these drugs break the rapid loop causing supraventricular tachycardia. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T3#GNS223_U1_T3_h6)

question: What is the primary clinical use for an intravenous dose of adenosine?

options.B: Thinning the blood to prevent sudden stroke events
options.C: Treating severe high blood pressure in the emergency room
options.D: Reversing a dangerous potassium overdose in the kidneys

explanation: Adenosine has a tiny half-life and is slammed fast intravenously to briefly stop AV node conduction and reset a fast rhythm. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T3#GNS223_U1_T3_h7)

question: Which patient sensation is commonly reported immediately after receiving a fast IV push of adenosine?

options.A: Severe numbness and tingling in both legs and feet
options.B: A brief feeling of the heart pausing or chest pressure
options.C: Sudden uncontrollable shaking in the hands and arms
options.D: An intense craving for cold water and sweet foods

explanation: Adenosine momentarily stops electrical conduction through the heart, which patients often experience as a frightening pause or thump. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T3#GNS223_U1_T3_h7)

question: Why is checking electrolyte levels like potassium and magnesium vital before giving antiarrhythmics?

options.A: Vitamins and minerals completely cancel out the side effects of antiarrhythmics
options.B: Electrolytes determine how fast the kidneys filter the drug out of the body
options.C: Low minerals cause the intravenous tubing to clog up during administration
options.D: Abnormal electrolyte levels can make the heart more prone to dangerous rhythms

explanation: Electrolyte imbalances directly affect cardiac cell stability and can trigger or worsen arrhythmias despite medication. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T3#GNS223_U1_T3_h8)

question: A patient taking a new antiarrhythmic drug tells the nurse they feel dizzy and lightheaded. What is the best initial nursing action?

options.A: Tell the patient to stand up quickly to test their balance
options.B: Administer a dose of sublingual nitroglycerin for chest pain
options.C: Check the patient's current blood pressure and heart rate
options.D: Hold the next scheduled dose and discharge the patient home

explanation: Dizziness and lightheadedness can signal a sudden drop in blood pressure or a slow heart rate caused by the drug. [learn more](GNS223_U1_T3#GNS223_U1_T3_h8)
